v.h: Tech earnings rout sinks the Nasdaq about 3%; Intel falls 30%
v.s: The Nasdaq was down about 3.1% and the S&P 500 2.1% Friday afternoon. Intel fell about 30% after a weak fourth-quarter forecast that cited a PC slump and a factory accident in Israel, pulling AMD down 12% and Nvidia 5%; Amazon's results disappointed, and Reddit fell about 28% on a softer outlook. The Russell 2000 opened higher, and Regeneron, Veralto and CoStar rose on earnings beats.
v.w: A second straight day of big-tech losses is the main reason long rates fell this week; if AI spending doubts keep spreading, they help borrowers through lower Treasury yields even as they hurt REIT and lab tenants tied to tech.

v.h: 10-year falls toward 4.9%, capping its biggest monthly rally since 2024
v.s: The 10-year was about 4.93% Friday afternoon (Trading Economics), roughly 5 bp below Thursday's 4.98% close, after touching about 4.89%, the lowest since Sept 10. It is down about 36–40 bp in October from 5.29% on Sept 30, the biggest monthly drop since 2024, while the 2-year fell about 32 bp. Investors moved from tech stocks into Treasuries after Alphabet, Amazon and Intel results raised doubts about debt-funded AI spending.
v.w: The 10-year is now about 38 bp below its Oct 5 high of 5.31%; for a lender quoting off the 10-year, that is roughly a third of a point off fixed-rate debt since early October.

v.h: December hike odds slip to about 72% from 79%
v.s: Kalshi priced a 71.5% chance of a Dec 9 hike and Polymarket 72.5% on Friday at 11:26 AM ET, down from 79% on Kalshi on Thursday; CME FedWatch was also near 72% (Trading Economics). Kalshi put a January 2027 hike at about 26%, down from 33%. The move followed an in-line ECI report and the tech selloff.
v.w: A hike is still favored, so floating-rate and SOFR-based loans likely get more expensive in December, but the odds are now back to where they were before the Oct 28 meeting.

v.h: Employment costs rise 0.8% in Q3; private wage growth slowest since 2021
v.s: The Employment Cost Index rose 0.8% in the third quarter, as expected. Private-industry wages and salaries rose 3.1% from a year earlier, the slowest since early 2021, and total compensation 3.4%; benefits rose 3.9%, with employer health insurance costs up 6.4%. Real wages fell 0.6% over the year.
v.w: Cooling wage growth argues against a wage-driven inflation spiral, but falling real pay squeezes renters and retail spending.

v.h: Microsoft's $25B bond sale draws $115B of orders
v.s: Microsoft priced $25B of bonds in 10 tranches from 2 to 40 years on Oct 29, its first U.S. dollar bond sale since 2017. Orders reached $115B, 4.6 times the deal, and the 40-year priced 105 bp over Treasuries, up to 30 bp inside initial guidance; Alphabet's 40-year trades about 28 bp wider.
v.w: Strong demand for top-rated corporate debt shows investors still have cash for long bonds, but heavy AI borrowing competes with real estate for the same buyers.

v.h: Brent climbs back toward $112.50 after tanker attacks in the Strait of Hormuz
v.s: Brent was near $112.50 on Friday, up about 1.5% from Thursday, after tanker attacks and mine strikes in the Strait of Hormuz and Houthi strikes on Saudi Arabia; WTI was near $104.
v.w: Oil near $110+ keeps diesel and heating costs high into winter, a direct hit to owner-paid utilities and construction budgets.

v.h: Stalled Newton development site sells at foreclosure auction for $6.5M
v.s: Trillennium Services, a Newton demolition contractor, won 283 Melrose St. in Auburndale with a $6.5M bid, topping lender Dedham Institution for Savings' $6.4M opening bid on a $9.4M 2018 loan. Townhouse construction was halted in 2023 for unpermitted work; the site carries about $16M of liens and fines and sits in Newton's Village Center Overlay District.
v.w: Another lender loss on a suburban residential site; the overlay zoning may let a new owner build more density than the stalled plan.

v.h: Boston's Hyatt Centric Faneuil Hall trades for $58.4M
v.s: EOS Investors of New York bought the 163-room hotel at 50–68 Devonshire St. from Magna Hospitality for $58.4M, about $358K per room, with $40M of Beacon Bank & Trust financing. Magna paid $16.5M in 2016 when Related sold the hotel portion of Congress Square.
v.w: Downtown hotels are still drawing outside capital and bank debt at a time when office in the same area sells at deep discounts.

v.h: 'Distress is finally trading': investors chase Boston office discounts
v.s: Boston office sales reached $2.2B in Q3, up 23.7% from a year earlier (Avison Young). Recent trades include 18 Tremont St. for $30M (Jamestown paid $103M in 2019), 10–20 Channel Center St. for $52M ($119M in 2016) and 100 Summer St. for $260M ($806M in 2019). Trepp counts $78B of CMBS loans reaching hard maturity from October 2026 through 2027.
v.w: Price discovery is happening deal by deal; these comps reset values for downtown office and the loans behind them.

v.h: High-yield spread widens 12 bp to 326 bp as tech stocks slide
v.s: The ICE BofA high-yield spread rose to 326 bp on Oct 29 from 314 bp a day earlier, and the investment-grade spread to 89 bp from 86 bp, as Alphabet's drop hit tech stocks. Both remain below their Oct 23 levels of 338 bp and 91 bp.
v.w: Credit spreads move with stocks; a wider spread can offset part of the Treasury rally in the all-in cost of riskier debt.

v.h: December hike odds rise to about 79% after the Fed's split vote
v.s: Kalshi priced a 79% chance of a Dec 9 hike on Thursday morning (11:27 AM ET), up from 72.5% on Oct 26 evening, and Polymarket was 76.5%; futures were near 85% after Wednesday's decision (Bloomberg data). Kalshi put a January 2027 hike at about 33% and March at about 54%. In-line PCE inflation on Thursday did not change the picture: markets still price a better-than-80% chance of a December move.
v.w: A December hike to 4.00–4.25% now looks likely, which would lift SOFR-based floating-rate loan costs by another 25 bp heading into 2027.

v.h: 10-year falls 7 bp to 4.98% as PCE comes in line and GDP beats
v.s: The 10-year closed at 4.98% on Thursday by Treasury's measure, down 7 bp from Wednesday's 5.05% and 2 bp below last Friday; the 2-year fell 6 bp to 4.61% and the 30-year 5 bp to 5.32%. September PCE prices rose 3.6% from a year earlier and core 3.1%, both in line with forecasts, while Q3 GDP grew at a 3.4% annual rate vs. 3.2% expected. Treasury sold $44B of 7-year notes at 4.894%, right on the when-issued level, with a 2.46x bid-to-cover.
v.w: The 10-year is back under 5%, but it has moved in a narrow 4.96–5.05% band for six sessions; with a December hike largely priced, loan quotes are unlikely to drop much before Dec 9.

v.h: Brent falls about 3% to near $111.50 on U.S. outreach to Iran
v.s: Brent traded near $111.50 late Thursday, down about $3.80 from Wednesday's $115.32 settlement, after the Wall Street Journal reported that Vice President JD Vance sent a letter to Iranian security chief Mohsen Rezaei aimed at reviving talks. President Trump said he did not direct the letter and that it concerned humanitarian aid. The Journal also reported Washington had warned Gulf states to prepare for a possible renewed campaign against Iran after the Nov 3 midterms.
v.w: Cheaper oil would ease diesel, heating oil and construction costs, but the post-election strike risk keeps energy prices volatile into the heating season.

v.h: Alphabet drops 12% and the Nasdaq falls 1.4%; Microsoft launches a $25B+ bond sale
v.s: The Nasdaq fell 1.38% to 26,184.72 and the S&P 500 0.31% to 7,720.10 after Alphabet sank more than 12% on a search revenue miss, while the Russell 2000 rose 1.0% and 8 of 11 S&P sectors gained. Microsoft beat forecasts and launched at least $25B of bonds in 10 tranches from 2 to 40 years, its first U.S. bond sale since 2017. Amazon reported after the close: EPS of $1.89 vs. $1.97 expected.
v.w: AI spenders are borrowing heavily in the bond market, adding corporate supply that competes with real estate debt for the same investors.

v.h: Freddie Mac 30-year rate falls to 7.24%, the lowest this month
v.s: The 30-year fixed averaged 7.24% this week, down from 7.32% and the second straight weekly decline; the 15-year fell to 6.60% from 6.68%. A year ago the 30-year was 6.17%. Mortgage News Daily's daily index was 7.35% on Oct 28.
v.w: Lower rates help condo and small multifamily buyers at the margin, but rates still 107 bp above a year ago keep would-be buyers renting longer.

v.h: Greater Boston pending home sales fall 10.6% in September
v.s: Agents reported 3,374 newly pending sales of all home types in September, 10.6% fewer than a year earlier, as the average 30-year mortgage rate ended the month at 7.28%, up from 6.65% at the end of August.
v.w: Slower for-sale activity keeps households in the rental pool, which supports apartment occupancy around Boston.

v.h: Fed holds at 3.75–4.00%, but two officials vote for a hike
v.s: The Fed left its target range at 3.75–4.00% in a 10–2 vote; Governor Lisa Cook and Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack dissented in favor of a quarter-point hike. The statement upgraded growth to "strong" from "solid" and dropped language tying policy to a return to 2% inflation. Chair Warsh called the hikes so far "monetary medicine starting to work some" but said there were "no firm conclusions," and that he is "unwilling and unable to call" financial conditions tight. The 10-year rose 6 bp to 5.05% on the day.
v.w: Two hike dissents show the committee leaning toward more tightening, so Boston and NH borrowers should expect no relief on short-term rates this year.

v.h: High-yield spread narrows 24 bp in three sessions to 314 bp
v.s: The ICE BofA high-yield spread fell to 314 bp on Oct 28 from 338 bp on Oct 23 and 340 bp on Oct 22; the investment-grade spread narrowed to 86 bp from 91 bp. The high-yield yield was 7.96% on Oct 27, down from 8.14% on Oct 23.
v.w: Tighter spreads lower all-in borrowing costs even with Treasuries flat, and improve the backdrop for CMBS and CRE CLO issuance.

v.h: South Weymouth air base plan readies a first phase of up to 2,700 homes
v.s: New England Development and Brookfield Properties, master developers since 2020, plan up to 2,700 units across 13 parcels in the first phase of the 1,400-acre site, with two apartment complexes set to start in March 2027. A $120M, 6.7-mile MWRA water pipeline is due by 2032; MassDevelopment and MassWorks have committed $35M over two years for water, sewer and roads.
v.w: A large new South Shore rental pipeline would add competition for Weymouth and Braintree apartments later this decade.

v.h: Rockpoint buys back 100 Summer St. for $260M at foreclosure, 68% below its 2019 price
v.s: Rockpoint Group, the existing owner, was the only bidder at Tuesday's foreclosure auction of the 32-story, roughly 1.1M SF tower near South Station, paying the $260M opening bid, about $236/SF. Rockpoint paid $806M in 2019 with $470M of Wells Fargo financing. The building is 72% occupied; tenants include SimpliSafe and the Massachusetts Trial Court.
v.w: A third high-profile distressed downtown sale since early 2025 resets the price benchmark for older Class A towers to about a quarter of replacement-era values.

v.h: Alexandria to sell its unfinished 421 Park Drive lab tower in the Fenway
v.s: Alexandria Real Estate Equities agreed to sell the 13-story, 339,668 SF building to an unnamed institutional investor, with closing expected in Q4 2026; no price was disclosed. The buyer is expected to take on about $136M of remaining interior lab work. About 268,000 SF was sold to Boston Children's Hospital in 2023 as a condominium.
v.w: Even the largest lab owner is shedding development risk, a sign that Boston life science values have not found a floor.

v.h: Case-Shiller: home prices up 2.1% in August; Boston up 2.6%
v.s: The national index rose 2.1% from a year earlier in August (1.9% in July) and the 20-city composite 2.7%. Boston rose 2.6% over the year but fell 0.35% on the month. Chicago (+6.7%) led; Seattle (−2.0%) was weakest. Real home prices fell for a 15th straight month.
v.w: Flat real home prices and 7%+ mortgages keep ownership costly relative to renting in Greater Boston.

v.h: 5-year auction: $70B at 4.845% with firmer demand than September
v.s: Treasury sold $70B of 5-year notes at 4.845% with a 0.4 bp tail (0.9 bp average). The bid-to-cover was 2.33x vs. 2.21x in September; dealers took 10.6% vs. a 13.0% average. On Wednesday the $28B 2-year FRN drew a 3.05x bid-to-cover at a 0.038% high margin.
v.w: Steady demand at the belly of the curve, where most 5-year CRE loans are priced, eases fears of a buyers' strike.

v.h: Diesel rises 7.6¢ to $6.352; New England gasoline dips to $4.199
v.s: EIA's Oct 26 survey showed U.S. diesel up 7.6¢ to $6.352, $2.634 above a year ago, and regular gasoline down 1.5¢ to $4.269. In New England, diesel fell 4.9¢ to $6.421 and gasoline 5.0¢ to $4.199; Boston gasoline was $4.176.
v.w: Diesel near $6.40 in New England keeps construction, trucking and heating oil costs high for owners into winter.

v.h: 10-year holds at 5.00% as the $69B 2-year auction tails
v.s: The 10-year closed at 5.00% on Monday by Treasury's measure, unchanged from Friday and 15 bp below its 5.15% close a week earlier, after the Oct 22 flight-to-safety drop. The 2-year was 4.68% and the 30-year 5.31%. Treasury sold $69B of 2-year notes at 4.708%, a 0.3 bp tail, with a 2.59x bid-to-cover vs. a 2.64x average; dealers took 13.0% vs. an 11.3% average.
v.w: Yields have held most of last week's drop, but a soft start to $211B of note sales this week shows demand is still price-sensitive heading into the Fed decision.

v.h: Brent slips to $115.81 as mediators meet Iranian officials in Tehran
v.s: Brent settled at $115.81, down 91 cents, and WTI at $101.76, down $1.51, on hopes that talks in Tehran involving Qatari mediators and Saudi, Turkish and Pakistani officials could ease hostilities. Houthi attacks on Saudi pumping stations and reports that U.S. forces could strike Iran within 96 hours of an order limited the decline.
v.w: Oil near $116 still feeds diesel, heating oil and construction costs; a diplomatic breakthrough would be the clearest path to lower inflation and yields.

v.h: Anthropic files public S-1 for Nasdaq IPO; Nasdaq rises 0.8%
v.s: Anthropic made its S-1 public on Monday to list on the Nasdaq under the ticker ANT, with 22 banks led by Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley; the price range is still blank. The filing shows first-half revenue of $16.3B and a mostly non-cash $80.7B net loss. The Wall Street Journal reported a listing targeted for the week of Nov 16, and people familiar with the matter said it could raise $100B or more. The S&P 500 rose 0.7% to 7,676.77 and the Nasdaq 0.8% to 26,169.38. Separately, Meta said it plans to raise up to $95B in stock for AI data centers.
v.w: A record-size equity raise, plus Meta's stock sale, shows AI spending shifting toward equity funding, which could ease some of the pressure on credit markets that has kept CRE loan spreads wide.

v.h: October hike odds hold near 7%; December near 73%
v.s: Kalshi priced a 7.5% chance of an Oct 28 hike and Polymarket 6.5% on Monday evening, down about 6 points over the week. Kalshi's December contract was about 72.5% for a hike, and the odds of at least one more hike before 2027 were 77%.
v.w: A hold this week is widely expected; the December call, and the 10-year, still hinge on Thursday's PCE inflation data and oil.

v.h: Eastern Bank reports record income growth in Q3
v.s: Eastern Bank said overall income rose 50% in the third quarter and net interest income rose by more than $57M.
v.w: Strong earnings at a large local lender support its capacity to make commercial real estate loans in Greater Boston.

v.h: Flash PMI: selling prices rise at the fastest pace in more than four years
v.s: S&P Global's flash October manufacturing PMI rose to 56.0 from 55.9, above the 55.5 expected, while services fell to 57.9 from 58.8 and the composite to 57.6 from 58.4. The survey showed the sharpest increase in selling prices in more than four years as oil costs spread through goods and services.
v.w: Firm activity and faster price increases argue against a growth scare and keep a December hike on the table.

v.h: IG spread widens to 91 bp; high-yield eases to 338 bp
v.s: The ICE BofA investment-grade spread rose to 91 bp on Oct 23 from 89 bp, its fifth straight daily increase, and the IG yield rose to 5.84%. The high-yield spread eased 2 bp to 338 bp, with the HY yield at 8.14%.
v.w: Wider corporate spreads tend to show up in CRE loan quotes, offsetting part of the drop in Treasury yields.

v.h: Vigilant Holdings buys Londonderry industrial building for $16.6M
v.s: Vigilant Holdings bought 13 Page Rd. in Londonderry, a fully leased 75,480 SF Class A industrial building completed in 2025, from an affiliate of Rhino Capital Advisors for $16.6M, about $220/SF. Bar Harbor Bank & Trust provided an $11.45M five-year fixed-rate acquisition loan; JLL represented the seller.
v.w: JLL says the pricing gap between southern New Hampshire and gateway markets is narrowing, and local banks are still lending on new, leased industrial.

v.h: 24-unit Brighton apartment building sells for $8.875M
v.s: Marcus & Millichap closed the sale of 15 Euston Rd., a 24-unit building in Brighton, for $8.875M, about $370,000 per unit, after a record number of groups toured the property.
v.w: Deep buyer interest in small Boston multifamily contrasts with distress elsewhere in Brighton, such as the Selkirk Place foreclosure auction set for Oct 28.

v.h: Brent settles at $116.72 as fears of renewed U.S. strikes on Iran grow
v.s: Brent crude for December rose about 3.4% to settle at $116.72, its third straight weekly gain, and WTI traded near $104. Reports said U.S. and Israeli officials drew up plans for renewed strikes on Iran, the State Department ordered non-essential staff to leave, and Saudi Aramco reportedly told staff to evacuate its Dhahran headquarters.
v.w: Higher oil feeds diesel, heating oil and construction costs and keeps inflation high, which limits how far Thursday's bond rally can run.

v.h: FoxRock buys Quincy office building for $5.5M, 78% below its 2013 price
v.s: FoxRock Properties bought 1100 Crown Colony Drive in Quincy, a 132,000 SF office building, from W.P. Carey for $5.5M, per an Oct. 21 deed, about $42/SF. W.P. Carey paid $25.5M in 2013. Sole tenant Arbella Insurance is moving next door to 1200 Crown Colony, which FoxRock also owns.
v.w: A South Shore suburban office comp at about $42/SF shows how far single-tenant office values fall once the tenant leaves.

v.h: 10-year ends the week at 5.00%, 9 bp below the prior Friday
v.s: The 10-year closed at 5.00% on Friday by Treasury's measure, up 4 bp from Thursday's 4.96% close but 9 bp below the prior Friday's 5.09%. Stocks slipped: the S&P 500 fell 0.5% and the Dow 1.2%, while the Nasdaq dipped 0.2% after Thursday's 2.6% drop.
v.w: Treasuries held most of Thursday's rally despite higher oil, so long-term borrowing costs end the week lower going into $211B of note auctions and the Fed meeting.

v.h: Consumer sentiment revised up to 48.0, still a five-month low
v.s: The University of Michigan's final October sentiment index was 48.0, up from a preliminary 46.3 but below September's 48.1. Year-ahead inflation expectations were 4.7% and long-run expectations 3.5%, both up a tenth from September.
v.w: Weak sentiment with rising inflation expectations is the mix that keeps the Fed leaning toward a December hike while consumers pull back.

v.h: High-yield spread jumps 13 bp to 340 bp as Treasuries rally
v.s: The ICE BofA high-yield spread widened to 340 bp on Oct 22 from 327 bp the day before, and the investment-grade spread rose to 89 bp. All-in yields still fell as Treasuries rallied: the IG index yielded 5.79% and high yield 8.14%.
v.w: Wider spreads offset part of the drop in Treasury yields, so CRE loan rates fall less than the 10-year.

v.h: AI credit stress spreads: record junk spreads, CoreWeave and Oracle swaps near highs
v.s: Spreads on AI-related high-yield debt jumped 25 bp in a day to a record 360 bp over Treasuries while non-AI junk moved 2 bp. CoreWeave's 5-year CDS was about 1,066 bp on Oct 21 after a record near 1,195 bp on Oct 15; Oracle's was about 308 bp vs. 141 bp in January. AI-related debt issued in 2026 has passed $500B.
v.w: Stress at the biggest borrowers widens spreads for everyone, so loan quotes may not fall as much as Treasuries.

v.h: Blackstone: cap rates rose across its real estate in Q3; opportunistic funds fell 3.2%
v.s: Blackstone said valuation cap rates rose across its holdings in the third quarter on rate volatility. Opportunistic real estate funds fell 3.2% while core-plus gained 1.6%, and real estate distributable earnings fell 10% to $1.68B. Schwarzman said a higher cost of capital has hurt transaction activity.
v.w: The largest owner is marking values down on rates, which feeds the comps and appraisals lenders use for everyone else.

v.h: Lender schedules foreclosure auction for 30-unit Brighton apartment building
v.s: Selkirk Place Apartments, 56–58 Selkirk Place near Cleveland Circle, goes to auction Oct 28. The owner financed its $12.8M 2022 purchase with an $8.75M loan; the city assesses the building at $7.24M, and a recent listing at $12.5M was cancelled.
v.w: A 2022 Boston apartment purchase now assessed below its loan shows how far values have reset for owners who bought at peak prices with floating or short-term debt.

v.h: 10-year Treasury falls below 5% in a flight to safety
v.s: The 10-year yield fell about 17 bp to 4.96%, its biggest one-day drop in more than two years and first close under 5% since late September, as investors moved into bonds during an AI-spending selloff that sent the Nasdaq down 2.6% (its worst day since June) and the S&P 500 down 1.2%. The 5-year fell 17 bp to 4.78%, matching the 10-year; the 2-year fell to 4.65% and the 30-year to 5.29%. Meta fell about 7% after raising the low end of its 2026 capex range to $135B.
v.w: A sub-5% 10-year eases refinance and cap-rate math, but a move driven by risk-off selling can reverse quickly.

v.h: Freddie Mac 30-year rate falls to 7.32%
v.s: Freddie Mac's 30-year fixed averaged 7.32%, down from 7.40%, ending a seven-week run without a decline; the 15-year fell to 6.68%. A year ago the 30-year was 6.19%. Mortgage News Daily's index fell 10 bp to 7.30% on Thursday.
v.w: Slightly lower mortgage rates help condo and small-multifamily exits, but buyers are still paying over a point more than a year ago.

v.h: Brent tops $112 after drone attack on Saudi oilfield
v.s: Brent settled at $112.92, up about 3.8%, after Saudi Arabia said it intercepted a drone aimed at the Shaybah oilfield; debris killed two contractor workers. Reports that the U.S. and Israel are weighing new strikes on Iran added to the move, and WTI neared $100.
v.w: Higher oil feeds heating, diesel and construction input costs for New England owners heading into winter.

v.h: October hike odds fall to about 6%; December near 72%
v.s: Kalshi and Polymarket both priced about a 5.5% chance of an Oct 28 hike on Thursday afternoon, down 23 points in a week. Kalshi's December contract fell to about 72% for a hike from 80% on Oct 20.
v.w: A pause next week is now nearly priced in, though a December increase remains the base case for floating-rate borrowers.

v.h: Jobless claims fall to 194,000, lowest since July
v.s: Initial jobless claims fell to 194,000 from 200,000, the fewest in three months; the four-week average was 197,750. Weekly claims have not topped 230,000 this year.
v.w: Low layoffs support tenant demand and rent collections even as hiring stays slow.

v.h: 5-year TIPS auction clears at 2.367%, highest real yield in three years
v.s: Treasury sold $26B of new 5-year TIPS at a 2.367% real yield, slightly above the 2.36% when-issued level; bid-to-cover was 2.41, the lowest for a similar sale since April 2025. The implied 5-year inflation breakeven was about 2.41%.
v.w: High real yields, not inflation expectations, are what keep borrowing costs elevated for real estate.

v.h: Debt-sale delays top $5B, including Freddie Mac apartment-loan bonds
v.s: Companies postponed more than $5B of U.S. and European debt sales in October, the most this year. Freddie Mac pulled more than $440M of bonds backed by apartment mortgages and Mesirow shelved $175M of bonds tied to a Manhattan office tower. U.S. junk issuance fell to about $7B in October from $51B in September.
v.w: When agency apartment securitizations can't clear at target prices, multifamily loan spreads widen even as Treasuries rally.

v.h: 20-year bond reopening sells at 5.469% with a small tail
v.s: Treasury sold $13B of 20-year bonds at 5.469%, about 0.9 bp above the when-issued level. Bid-to-cover was 2.73 vs. a 2.62 average; directs took 31.6%, indirects 58.2% and dealers 10.3%.
v.w: Steady demand for long Treasuries helps cap long-term rates that drive permanent loan pricing.

v.h: Massachusetts constraints push more apartment investors to southern NH
v.s: Bisnow reports developers and investors are shifting to the I-93 corridor: Procopio is preparing a 310-unit build-to-rent project in Londonderry with a Rockland Trust construction loan, and Passco, TA Realty and Harbor Group have bought large Salem, Merrimack and Nashua communities. Colliers put NH apartment occupancy at 95.4% and average asking rent at $2,292, up 1.1%.
v.w: More capital and 4,000+ new units in southern NH mean more competition for acquisitions and softer rent growth in the region.

v.h: BGO buys leased Wrentham warehouse for $34.9M
v.s: BGO bought 545 Washington St. in Wrentham, a 132,055 SF Class A industrial building completed in 2023 and 100% leased to two tenants, from Bluewater Property Group and Affinius Capital. JLL represented the sellers.
v.w: About $264/SF for new, leased South Shore-area distribution is a fresh pricing marker for Route 1/I-495 industrial.

v.h: Liberty Mutual plans 85,000 SF Back Bay HQ expansion
v.s: Liberty Mutual filed a letter of intent to demolish three buildings on Stuart St. and Columbus Ave. and add a 23K SF vertical addition plus a 62K SF, 10-story building next to 157 Berkeley St. It plans to lease out its offices at 175 Berkeley St. and 30 St. James Ave. after consolidating.
v.w: Two large Back Bay office blocks coming to market would add sublease and direct supply to an already high-vacancy office market.

v.h: Poll: 65% back Question 7 to limit large minimum lot sizes
v.s: A UMass Amherst/WCVB poll found 65% of Massachusetts voters support the starter-homes ballot question, up from 59% in August, with 21% opposed and 10% undecided.
v.w: If it passes on Nov 3, smaller-lot zoning could open more suburban land for housing development.

v.h: Housing starts fall 5.2% in September to a 1.221M pace
v.s: Census said starts dropped to a 1.221M annual rate from a revised 1.288M in August, below the 1.310M consensus. Single-family starts fell 4.6% to 859,000, buildings with five or more units ran at 349,000, and permits slipped 0.2% to 1.400M.
v.w: Fewer starts with mortgages above 7% means less new supply competing with existing apartments in 2027–28.

v.h: 10-year eases to about 5.12% as oil reverses on Iran diplomacy hopes
v.s: Brent touched $111.99 after attacks on Gulf shipping, then settled at $108.79, down about 0.7%, on reports mediators were exploring a framework to revive U.S.-Iran talks; no breakthrough was confirmed. The 10-year fell about 2 bp to roughly 5.12%, helped by weak housing data, after rising to 5.15% on Monday.
v.w: Oil is still the swing factor for inflation and long rates, so cap-rate and refinancing math stays tied to Gulf headlines.

v.h: October hike odds slip to about 13%; December near 80%
v.s: Kalshi priced a 12.5% chance of an Oct 28 hike and Polymarket 13.5% on Tuesday evening, down 6 points over the week. Kalshi's December contract showed about 80% for a hike, and the odds of at least one more hike in 2026 were about 81%.
v.w: A pause next week is the base case, but floating-rate and bridge borrowers should still budget for a December increase.

v.h: Somerville 120-unit portfolio sells for $39M
v.s: Three brick apartment buildings at 18 Day St., 49 Dover St. and 123 Orchard St. near Davis Square sold for $39M (about $325,000 per unit) after more than three rounds of bidding. Matthews represented the seller, which had held the buildings for more than a century; the buyer was not named.
v.w: Competitive bidding for older Red Line-adjacent apartments shows deep buyer demand for well-located Boston-area multifamily despite 5% Treasury yields.

v.h: Copper Mill sues partners over collapsed 754-unit Dorchester project
v.s: Copper Mill filed a nine-count suit in Suffolk Superior Court against site owners POB Capital and Pactolus Private Wealth Management over 75 Morrissey Blvd., a BPDA-approved two-tower, 754-unit plan. It alleges the owners moved to end their joint venture after the $67.5M purchase agreement while pursuing a deal valuing the site at $82.5M.
v.w: Another large approved Boston apartment project is stuck, which keeps new supply along Morrissey Blvd. further out.

v.h: Marcus & Millichap sees Boston office vacancy dipping to 19.1%
v.s: The firm expects metro vacancy to fall 10 bp year over year to 19.1% in Q4, the first annual decline since 2022, with asking rents up 1.2% to $38.75/SF. Cambridge vacancy rose 250 bp to 22.8%; average sale pricing fell from over $370/SF in 2022 to about $283/SF, with cap rates up from 6.7% to 7.7%.
v.w: Office pricing near $283/SF and 7.7% caps sets the bar for value-add and conversion bids.

v.h: Greystar opens 416-unit Juniper, last piece of its Everett build-out
v.s: Juniper at 201 Mill Road is Greystar's fifth and final community in Everett's Commercial Triangle, an $880M redevelopment totaling 1,905 apartments and 6,500 SF of retail. Construction began in summer 2024 and topped off in December 2025.
v.w: Another 416 units leasing up north of Boston adds near-term competition for Class A rents in Everett, Malden and Chelsea.

v.h: Troubled $22.4M office loan lifts Rockland Trust's bad loans 45%
v.s: Rockland Trust said nonperforming loans rose to $125.7M from $86.5M a year earlier, driven by a $22.4M office loan in workout whose tenant left; the building could become apartments. Delinquent loans rose to 0.73% of loans from 0.49%.
v.w: Local banks are still working through office problems, which keeps their CRE lending terms tight.

v.h: Mortgage rates start the week higher at 7.43%
v.s: Mortgage News Daily's 30-year index rose 6 bp to 7.43% on Oct 19; FHA was 7.04% and VA 7.05%. Freddie Mac's weekly average was 7.40% on Oct 15.
v.w: Mortgages above 7.4% keep would-be buyers renting, which supports apartment occupancy.

v.h: Nuveen: Treasuries rallied last week while credit spreads widened
v.s: Nuveen's weekly commentary said the 10-year fell 17 bp to 5.08% in the week to Oct 16, while the investment-grade spread widened to 84 bp, high yield to 331 bp and CMBS to 71 bp as some issuers postponed deals after hot inflation data.
v.w: Wider CMBS spreads offset part of the drop in Treasury yields, so all-in CRE loan coupons fell less than the 10-year.

v.h: Rate jump clouds Greater Boston apartment sales
v.s: Banker & Tradesman reports investment sales picked up after the SJC struck rent control from the ballot in June, but brokers say buyers can absorb only about 25–30 bp of rate moves and the 10-year rose above 5.2%. Regional occupancy stayed above 95% and units under construction fell to 8,221 from more than 17,000 at the 2022 peak (Colliers).
v.w: Falling construction supports rents, but rate volatility is widening bid-ask spreads on multifamily trades.

v.h: Rising rates cloud Greater Boston apartment sales
v.s: Investment sales picked up after the rent control question was removed from the ballot in June, then slowed as rates rose; CBRE's Simon Butler said most buyers can absorb 25 to 30 bp of rate movement. Colliers counts 8,221 units under construction, down from more than 17,000 at the 2022 peak.
v.w: With the 10-year above 5%, bid-ask gaps on Boston multifamily are widening again, though the shrinking pipeline supports rents later.

v.h: Boston investor buys 13-tenant Nashua industrial building
v.s: Sticks Investment Group bought the fully leased 46,869 SF small-bay building at 4 Bud Way in Nashua from JP Irvine LLC in an off-market deal; Hunneman represented the buyer and Colliers the seller. The price was not disclosed.
v.w: Boston capital is moving into southern NH small-bay industrial, a sign of demand for multi-tenant flex there.

v.h: Warsh gives no rate signal at IMF meeting
v.s: Speaking at an IMF meeting in Bangkok, Fed Chair Kevin Warsh declined to signal whether the Fed will raise rates on Oct 27–28, saying he does not prejudge decisions; the Fed's pre-meeting quiet period began Saturday.
v.w: With no guidance before the meeting, data and oil will drive rate expectations into Oct 28.

v.h: Prof G Markets: is the AI build-out a replay of the 1873 railroad crash?
v.s: Financial historian Liaquat Ahamed tells Ed Elson the data-center boom echoes the post-Civil War railroad mania, when U.S. track mileage doubled in seven years, mostly on borrowed money, until Jay Cooke's bank failed in 1873 and about a third of railroad bonds stopped paying within two years. His warning signs today: AI spending estimates that keep rising, hyperscalers turning to debt, private credit and special-purpose vehicles, and cash-hungry AI labs that may struggle to raise money. He thinks the line into excess may already be behind us, but expects the technology to outlast any bust, as railroads did, with patient capital the long-run winner.
v.w: A debt-funded AI pullback would hit private credit and data-center lenders first, which could tighten credit for CRE borrowers; the GPU rental-rate signal on the trading tab is meant to catch that early.

v.h: 10-year yield edges up Friday but ends the week about 14 bp lower
v.s: The 10-year Treasury yield was about 5.09% Friday afternoon, up slightly on the day, after closing at 5.10% on Oct 15. It remains below early-October highs, which were the highest since 2002; the 30-year was about 5.43%.
v.w: A week of lower long rates gives a little room on refinancing and cap-rate math, but the 10-year is still above 5%.

v.h: October hike odds fall to about 14%; December still ~77%
v.s: Kalshi priced a 15% chance of an Oct 28 hike and Polymarket 13.5% on Friday afternoon, down from 29% on Wednesday evening. A December hike is still favored at about 77%.
v.w: An October pause is now the base case, but floating-rate borrowers should still plan for a December increase.

v.h: Boston backs tax deals to unlock ~1,400 stalled apartments
v.s: The BPDA board approved Chapter 121B tax agreements for four projects in Charlestown and Allston-Brighton, including Fulcrum's 408-unit One Mystic Ave. and Hines' 318-unit 22-24 Pratt St. Taxes are frozen during construction and phased in over five or 10 years; abatements total about $31.5M.
v.w: Adds future rental supply in Boston and shows the city will use tax relief to get financing-starved projects moving; 10 to 12 more could qualify.

v.h: Industrial production rises 0.7% in September
v.s: Output rose 0.7%, the most in five months and above the ~0.4% forecast. Manufacturing rose 0.3% and utilities jumped 3.5% in a record-warm September.
v.w: Another firm reading that keeps a December Fed hike in play.

v.h: IEA says the diesel shortage will last into 2027
v.s: Oil headed for a weekly gain on Middle East supply risks; the IEA said diesel inventories are not expected to recover until the second half of 2027. G7 members agreed to release 100 million barrels of diesel and other reserves.
v.w: Keeps construction hauling, heating oil and building operating costs elevated through the coming winter.

v.h: Turner: building costs up 5.49% from a year ago in Q3
v.s: The Turner Building Cost Index rose 1.48% in the third quarter to 1,575, up 5.49% from a year earlier, driven by data center, chip-plant and campus work, short supplies of mechanical and electrical trades, and renewed material price pressure.
v.w: Higher replacement cost supports existing buildings' values and keeps new apartment starts scarce.

v.h: Manchester property values jump 48% in revaluation
v.s: Preliminary revaluation figures put Manchester's total value at $23.09B, up 48% over five years. Three-family buildings rose 74% and four-plus-unit apartment buildings 58%, while commercial, industrial and condo values rose less than average.
v.w: The tax rate should fall, but apartment owners will likely carry a bigger share of the levy while commercial owners may see smaller bills.

v.h: 30-year mortgage rate holds at 7.40%, ending a seven-week climb
v.s: Freddie Mac's 30-year average was unchanged at 7.40%; the 15-year slipped to 6.71% from 6.73%. A year ago the 30-year was 6.27%. Mortgage News Daily's index eased to 7.37% on Oct 16.
v.w: Rates near 7.4% keep would-be buyers renting, which supports apartment demand but slows condo and for-sale exits.

v.h: Boston ranks among the nation's tightest retail markets
v.s: Boston-area retail vacancy was 3.5% in Q3 vs. 4.9% nationally, per Marcus & Millichap. New retail deliveries this year are expected to be the lowest since 2007, and good Back Bay, Seaport, Fenway or suburban sites draw five or six offers.
v.w: Supports rent growth and occupancy for well-located retail, including ground-floor space in mixed-use assets.

v.h: $850M financing closes for Chelsea battery storage project
v.s: Flatiron Energy closed about $850M of construction and term financing for the 1,200 MWh Energizar battery storage project in Chelsea, led by Nord LB, Santander and Société Générale. Operations are expected in Q4 2027.
v.w: Large grid storage near Boston could ease local power constraints over time; lenders are still funding big energy infrastructure.

v.h: Wholesale prices jump 6.3% as fuel costs surge
v.s: September PPI rose 1.3% on the month, the most since March 2022 and above the ~0.6% forecast, and 6.3% over the year. Goods rose 2.6%, led by energy (+10.8%); core PPI rose 0.5% (5.0% y/y).
v.w: Feeds directly into construction and operating costs and adds to the case for another Fed hike.

v.h: 10-year yield drops to about 5.05% despite the hot PPI
v.s: The 10-year Treasury yield fell about 13 bp to roughly 5.05% on Oct 15 and the 30-year to about 5.40%, as a global equity sell-off pushed money into bonds.
v.w: A lower 10-year eases refinancing math, but one day's rally doesn't change a 5%-plus rate backdrop.

v.h: Retail sales rise 0.8% in September, beating forecasts
v.s: Sales rose 0.8% vs. 0.3% expected, with August revised to +1.3%. Excluding gas stations, sales rose only 0.2%; department stores rose 1.6% and restaurants 1.1%.
v.w: Much of the gain is gasoline prices, so underlying demand for retail tenants is softer than the headline.

v.h: CIM sells Back Bay's Motor Mart Garage, reportedly for about $89M
v.s: Related Beal and Freeport Equity bought the 1,037-space garage at 201 Stuart St. with about 49K SF of retail; the Globe reported $89M. CIM paid $162.5M in 2016 and never built its approved 306-unit tower.
v.w: A roughly 45% loss on a prime Back Bay site shows how far values have reset when development math no longer works.

v.h: Boston Fed Beige Book: CRE steady, but loans got costlier and tighter
v.s: Activity in the district expanded slightly. Office leasing rose slowly and vacancies dipped, industrial was flat, and construction slowed; financing costs rose and loan terms tightened.
v.w: A direct read on New England lending conditions: steady fundamentals, but tighter credit and rising long rates.

v.h: October hike odds ease to about 29% by Wednesday evening
v.s: After jumping to about 36% at midday on the CPI report, Kalshi and Polymarket priced roughly a 29% chance of an Oct 28 hike by 7 PM ET; December stayed near 78%.
v.w: Markets still expect another hike by December, keeping floating-rate debt costs elevated.

v.h: Chestnut Hill Realty puts 56-unit Brookline building on the market
v.s: Boston Realty Advisors is marketing Beacon Fairbanks Manor, a fully rented, market-rate 1910 building at Beacon and Fairbanks streets next to a Green Line stop.
v.w: A rare transit-oriented Brookline multifamily offering that will help mark local per-unit pricing.

v.h: $16M+ in public money lined up for Hyde Park's Fairmount Apartments
v.s: Federal, state and city funds will start modernizing the 200-plus-unit public housing complex built in 1951, including electrified heat and hot water and added cooling.
v.w: Shows state and city money flowing to preservation and electrification in Boston's existing housing stock.

v.h: Portsmouth housing authority seeks ideas for 17-acre Swanson Homes site
v.s: PRHA is holding sessions on the former public housing site, demolished in June, where it wants mixed use; private developers have shown no interest so far and a HUD grant was not awarded.
v.w: A sizable in-town Portsmouth parcel that could come to market as a public-private development opportunity.

v.h: Inflation climbs to 3.7% as gasoline jumps; core runs hotter than expected
v.s: September CPI rose 0.6% on the month and 3.7% from a year earlier, above the 3.6% forecast. Core prices rose 0.3% (2.6% y/y) vs. 0.2% expected, with gasoline up 9.1% and shelter up 0.4%.
v.src: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics / Yahoo Finance
v.w: Keeps pressure on long rates and loan pricing two weeks before the Fed meets.

v.h: Odds of an October Fed hike roughly double after CPI
v.s: Polymarket priced a 47.5% chance of an Oct. 28 hike shortly after the release, up from about 18% a day earlier; by midday the Kalshi/Polymarket average sat near 36%, with December near 79%. The 10-year touched about 5.30% before easing to around 5.24%.
v.src: DeFi Rate / Rio Times / Trading Economics
v.w: A hike this month would raise floating-rate debt costs and push refinancing relief further out.

v.h: WinnCompanies finishes 56-unit Eastwalk in Braintree
v.s: WinnCompanies and Arch Communities completed The Eastwalk, a $47M, five-story, 56-unit mixed-income building on the former Braintree Electric Light Department plant site along the Monatiquot River.
v.w: New transit-oriented supply on the South Shore at roughly $840K per unit shows today's development costs.

v.h: Medical anchor of 75K–100K SF eyed for Seacoast Landing in Newington
v.s: Torrington Properties' roughly $400M redevelopment of the former Mall at Fox Run on 82 acres already has Costco (opening by Thanksgiving 2027); a second large retailer is expected and demolition is about half complete.
v.w: A medical anchor would diversify the Seacoast's largest retail redevelopment beyond big-box tenants.

v.h: Investcorp buys eight Massachusetts industrial buildings for $76.5M
v.s: The Bahrain-based investor bought properties in Woburn, Marlborough, Randolph, Franklin and Westborough. Bisnow names Longfellow as the seller (bought for ~$62.3M in 2021–22); WBJ and Boston Real Estate Times name Longpoint Realty Partners.
v.w: Foreign capital is still paying up for I-495 industrial despite 5%+ Treasury yields.

v.h: NH bankers say the Fed's hike has barely touched the state economy
v.s: Citizens Bank's NH president said customers worry more about energy and health care costs than borrowing rates; Realtors report homes sitting longer and more price cuts as inventory rises.
v.w: Local demand is holding up, but rising inventory is starting to soften NH home pricing.

v.h: Gasoline and diesel ease slightly; New England diesel at $6.44
v.s: EIA's Oct. 12 survey put U.S. gasoline at $4.331 (down 2.3¢) and diesel at $6.179 (down 2.0¢), still $1.27 and $2.51 above a year ago. Boston gasoline was $4.305.
v.w: Fuel and heating costs remain a drag on operating budgets heading into winter.

v.h: Treasury yields ease as oil cools ahead of CPI
v.s: Bond trading resumed after Columbus Day with the 10-year down about 5 bp to roughly 5.19% and the 30-year near 5.56%. Brent eased toward $105 despite tanker incidents near Hormuz.
v.w: A small reprieve for loan pricing, but Wednesday's CPI decides whether it holds.

v.h: Nuveen pays $77M for 195-unit Revere Beach apartments
v.s: A TIAA-owned Nuveen affiliate bought One Beachmont from Redgate, about $395K a unit for a 2019 building by the Blue Line.
v.w: A fresh North Shore multifamily price point as institutional buyers return.

v.h: Marcus & Millichap: Boston office market shows signs of stabilizing
v.s: Suffolk County vacancy fell to 20.4% from 21.6% a year earlier with 1.3M SF of positive absorption in H1. Average pricing fell to about $283/SF from over $370 in 2022 as cap rates rose to 7.7% from 6.7%.
v.w: A reset office basis with improving absorption is starting to draw value buyers.

v.h: Kinepolis closes Showcase Cinemas deal, including seven MA theaters
v.s: The Belgian operator completed its acquisition of the National Amusements chain.
v.w: Theater-anchored retail centers get a new, better-capitalized operator.

v.h: Downtown Boston office vacancy dips to 18.5% in Q3
v.s: CBRE reports downtown vacancy of 18.5%, down from 18.7%, with leasing up to 1.27M SF (nearly 80% Class A) and net absorption of +62,741 SF, behind year-ago levels. Average asking rent slipped to $66.12/SF and nothing is under construction.
v.w: No new supply and steady Class A demand support well-located towers; older space still faces rent pressure.

v.h: Life Time plans 45K SF club at Commonwealth Pier in the Seaport
v.s: The athletic club operator will open its eighth Greater Boston location at 200 Seaport Blvd., redeveloped by Pembroke, in late 2027.
v.w: Experiential tenants are filling large Seaport space while office sublease supply grows.

v.h: 10-year auction prices at 5.30%, highest since 2000, but demand holds up
v.s: The S&P 500 gained 1.2% for the week and set a record early on, while bonds snapped a five-week losing streak after solid 10- and 30-year auctions.
v.w: Steady buyers at these yields eases fears of a disorderly spike in long rates.

v.h: Law firms push top Boston office rents to records
v.s: JLL's Q3 data puts top-tier high-rise rents at $105/SF, with Back Bay near $130, while the market-wide average asking rent slipped to $66.49.
v.w: The office market keeps splitting: trophy space tightens while older buildings lag.

v.h: NH ranks among the states with the fastest-rising mortgage rates
v.s: A new study puts New Hampshire ninth, adding pressure to an already tight housing market where permitting remains near historic lows.
v.w: Supports rental demand on the Seacoast and in southern NH.

TAKEAWAYS.label: Migration takeaways by generation
v: The biggest magnets have the softest rents

Dallas, Atlanta, Phoenix, Houston and Denver draw movers from all over, yet their rents are flat to falling and 55–67% of Zillow listings offer concessions: years of new supply are still being absorbed. Chicago and New York are the exception, with strong pull and rents up 4–5%. Low-pull Northeast and Rust Belt metros (Providence, Buffalo, Cleveland, Hartford) post solid gains on thin supply.
California and the Midwest lose the most

Counting out-of-state moves, California has the biggest net outflow, followed by Ohio, Oklahoma, Missouri and Michigan. Florida, Texas and Colorado gain the most. In New England, Massachusetts, Connecticut and Rhode Island run negative while New Hampshire gains, mostly from Boston.
Boomers head for sun and smaller places

Phoenix is the single biggest Boomer magnet, pulling from the whole West and Upper Midwest. Florida is the top state by a wide margin, followed by the Carolinas and Arizona. Retirement-style metros like Lake Havasu, Fort Myers, Prescott and Charleston rank high.
Gen X spreads across the Sun Belt
Dallas and Atlanta lead, followed by Chicago, Nashville, Tampa and Houston. Moves skew regional: Gen Xers often go a few hours away rather than across the country.

Texas is the top state for Millennials and Dallas is by far the top metro, ahead of Atlanta and Houston. They also move to nearby, cheaper metros like Worcester from Boston and Lehigh Valley from New York.
Gen Z moves back into big cities

New York City and Chicago draw Gen Z from nearly every region, and Denver, LA and the Bay Area follow. Older New Yorkers and Chicagoans, meanwhile, mostly head for the suburbs, Florida and the Sun Belt.
